summary:
TELLUS helps farmers decide what to plant after soybeans (corn, sorghum or a cover crop), using data to turn climate uncertainty into a traceable recommendation. The farmer marks the field, enters the harvest date and soil conditions, and TELLUS returns the options that fit the official planting window, each with its risk and expected margin.

We combine NASA GPM IMERG rainfall and NASA POWER data, validated against INMET ground stations, with ZARC rules and Conab production costs. The result ranks the planting options by margin and drought risk, always showing the sources behind every number.

This matters because second-crop decisions have to be made quickly, yet they depend on climate, soil, the planting calendar and costs. TELLUS makes that evidence understandable and auditable, so farmers can plant based on evidence, not guesswork.
details:
TELLUS is a web application developed for the Field Shift challenge of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps soybean farmers decide what to plant, and when, in the second-crop season, comparing options such as corn, sorghum and brachiaria grass. The tool was designed for use in Brazil, with Rio Verde, in the state of Goiás, as its reference case.

How it works. The farmer locates the field on the map, either through the Rural Environmental Registry (CAR, Brazil’s national land registry for rural properties) or by uploading a geographic file. Next, they enter the expected soybean harvest date, the soil characteristics and, if known, the cultivar maturity group. TELLUS cross-references this information with the official planting windows of the Agricultural Climate Risk Zoning (ZARC, Brazil’s official zoning that sets low-risk planting dates for each crop and municipality) and simulates the soil water balance using 25 years of historical data. For each eligible option, it shows the official risk, the simulated historical frequency of severe water deficit and, when enough economic data is available, the estimated margin per hectare under three scenarios.

Benefits and expected impact. The tool brings together data the farmer would otherwise have to look up in government ordinances, weather databases and cost spreadsheets. With it, farmers can compare the options for their own field and test how changes in harvest date, price or production cost affect the decision. Our goal is to make Earth observation data more accessible and to support second-crop planning in the face of rainfall and price variability.

Technologies and data. We built the backend in Python with FastAPI and Pydantic, and the interface with Astro, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet. We used GitHub Spec Kit to organize development, Claude Code and Codex to support implementation and testing, and Vitest and Playwright for automated tests. Historical rainfall comes from NASA GPM IMERG, cross-checked locally against an INMET weather station. NASA POWER provides the other meteorological variables, and economic data comes from Conab, Cepea and values entered by the farmer. The prototype runs locally on a regular computer, and the interface works in the browser on both desktop and mobile.

Creativity and factors considered. What sets TELLUS apart is that it starts from a concrete decision about a specific field and shows how each option was evaluated. The interface presents the official risk, the simulated historical risk and the economic margin separately. It also shows where every piece of data comes from and lets users change the assumptions to compare the original result with the adjusted one. The team took into account the quality and spatial resolution of the rainfall series, the soil’s water-holding capacity, the official planting windows and the availability of prices and costs for each crop. We also built the interface in both Portuguese and English.
dataRefs: NASA GPM IMERG Final Run V07B - Global Precipitation
projectRefs: MAPA (Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock): Agricultural Climate Risk Zoning (ZARC), including planting windows, official ordinances and soil available water capacity classes
INMET (Brazil’s National Institute of Meteorology): historical weather data, including automatic station A025 in Rio Verde, Goiás
IBGE (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics): Localities API, with municipality codes and names
SICAR (National Rural Environmental Registry System): WFS service with the boundaries of rural properties registered in the CAR
Conab (Brazil’s National Supply Company): agricultural production cost spreadsheets
Cepea/Esalq-USP (Center for Advanced Studies on Applied Economics, University of São Paulo): ESALQ/BM&FBovespa Corn Price Index
